lessons.title: How money works today
lessons.content:
# How money works today

This academy does not start with Bitcoin. It starts with the money you already use, because crypto is a response to that design — not a separate planet.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say, in your own words, what money is for, what a ledger is, what actually happens in a bank transfer, and why inflation and institutional trust matter. Those four ideas are the floor of everything later.

## Money is a tool with three jobs

A thing is treated as money when a group of people use it for three jobs. Economists give each job a name. We will use the names, then unpack them until they are usable.

**Medium of exchange**

This means: the thing people actually hand over when they trade. You do not have to find someone who both wants your bicycle and has the exact groceries you need. That failed matching problem is **barter**. Money exists so trade does not depend on a double coincidence of wants.

If a café will not accept concert tickets for coffee, those tickets are not a medium of exchange in that café. The medium of exchange is whatever the group already agrees to take.

**Store of value**

This means: you can keep the thing and still spend it later. A salary paid today is meant to still buy rent in two weeks. Food spoils. A service cannot sit in a drawer. Money is supposed to wait.

When it waits badly — when the same 100 units buy much less next year — that is a **store-of-value failure**. We will name that failure **inflation** later in this lesson. Hold the idea: storing is one of money’s jobs, and some forms of money do it worse than others.

**Unit of account**

This means: prices are written in it. A laptop costs 900 units, not “three favours and a used printer.” A shared measuring stick lets you compare one good with another, keep books, sign contracts, and tax income.

If something cannot do these three jobs well, people quietly stop treating it as money. That is why we do not price houses in birthday cakes.

TABLE
Job | Official name | What it means in practice
A way to trade | Medium of exchange | People accept it for goods and services
A way to keep | Store of value | It still works later
A way to measure | Unit of account | Prices, salaries, and debts are written in it
ENDTABLE

## Fiat money, cash, and bank money are not the same object

**Fiat money** is money that is money because a government and a legal system say it is, and because people actually use it — not because each note is a claim on a fixed weight of gold. The US dollar, the euro, the yen, the pound, and most national currencies you will meet are fiat.

That does not make them “fake.” It makes their value a social and political fact: laws, taxes, banks, and habit. Crypto later offers a different design (rules in public software). You cannot understand that offer if you think “real money” only means metal in a vault.

Your everyday “money” is also not one layer. It is a stack:

- **Cash** — notes and coins. Physical. Limited in practice. Easy to lose. Slow to move across a border.
- **Bank money** — numbers in an account. This is most of the money in a modern economy. It is a **promise** from a bank that they will honour withdrawals and payments under their rules.
- **Central-bank money** — the base layer. Commercial banks settle with each other through the central bank of that currency. You rarely touch this layer directly. It is still the foundation the other layers sit on.

When you tap a card or send a bank transfer, you are almost never mailing paper. You are asking two **ledgers** to change.

## A ledger is the book of who is owed what

A **ledger** is the official list of balances and transfers. A village savings group’s notebook is a ledger. A bank’s database is a ledger. A blockchain, later in this course, is also a ledger — with different rules about who may write, who may read, and how pages are sealed.

Your app “balance” is not a stack of notes with your name in a drawer. A few notes exist. Most money is an entry: the bank’s book says they owe you that amount, subject to law and their contract with you.

**Worked scenario.** You invoice a client for 2,000 units of your local currency. They pay by bank transfer.

1. Their bank checks: is the account open, is there enough, is the payment allowed.
2. If yes, their bank reduces the number on their page.
3. A clearing system — the plumbing between banks — carries the instruction.
4. Your bank increases the number on your page.
5. Your app shows a credit. You still cannot spend *cash* until you withdraw. What you have is a claim on your bank.

If any bookkeeper in that chain says no — fraud alert, frozen account, name mismatch, holiday window, sanctions list — the payment fails even though both of you “meant” it.

DIAGRAM
Payer’s bank ledger
        |
        v
Clearing / payment network
        |
        v
Your bank ledger
        |
        v
Your app shows a new balance

If any ledger says NO, you are not paid.
ENDDIAGRAM

TABLE
Layer | What you see | What it really is | Who can stop it
Cash | Notes in your hand | Physical fiat | Theft, loss, seizure
Bank deposit | App balance | A promise in the bank’s ledger | Bank, court, fraud team
Card / fintech wallet | Card or app | A company ledger, often sitting on banks underneath | The company, plus the banks behind it
ENDTABLE

## Inflation is a purchasing-power problem

**Inflation** means the general level of prices is rising, so each unit of money buys less. It is not a rumour and it is not only a Twitter argument.

Two honest drivers, without a conspiracy:

- Goods become scarcer (supply shock).
- More money chases the same goods (too much currency relative to output).

Families feel it as: “this salary does not finish the month.” That is a store-of-value complaint. People respond by converting idle cash into inventory, foreign currency, land, or financial assets. They are not all “traders.” They are trying to store value in something that shrinks more slowly.

Crypto culture talks about this constantly. Some overclaim. The useful beginner fact is calmer: **if a committee can create more of a money, that money has a political layer.** Whether that is good or bad is a debate. That it is true of major fiat currencies is not a debate.

Bitcoin’s designers later wanted a money whose **supply rules sat in public software** instead of a committee. You do not need Bitcoin yet. You need to see why anyone would want a different kind of ledger.

## Trust is the product banks actually sell

When you keep a salary in a bank, you are buying a bundle:

- a number you hope is real
- the hope the app works on Monday
- the hope a transfer does not vanish
- some chance that if a card is stolen, a bank or a scheme might reverse the payment

That bundle is **trust**. It is expensive to build. It is why banks ask who you are.

**KYC** means **Know Your Customer**: the institution records your identity because the law and their risk team require it. It is why some transfers have cut-off times. It is why sending money to another country can feel like paperwork — **correspondent banks**, compliance checks, and **SWIFT** messages (the messaging network banks use to instruct international payments, not a pile of cash flying across the ocean).

Crypto’s later bet is different: publish the rule-book and the ledger so you are not depending on one company’s database to know whether a transfer is valid. That bet has a cost. If you lose the secret that controls your coins, there is no “dear bank, reset my password.” This course will be honest about both sides.

NOTE
Academy rule: we will never tell you “fiat is fake” or “crypto replaces your bank tomorrow.” Adults use both. The skill is knowing what each layer can and cannot do. If a sentence uses a heavy word, the next paragraph must define it. If it does not, the course has failed — not you.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are not here to become an economist. You are here so that words like ledger, settlement, inflation, and KYC are tools, not fog. Module 2 will reuse them without apology. Module 3 will place tokens like Crystal Stones on top of them.

## Say this out loud

- Money is a tool with three jobs: trade, keep, measure.
- Most of the “money” in an app is not notes. It is a row in an institution’s book. That book is a ledger.
- A transfer is two ledgers changing. If a bookkeeper says no, you are not paid.
- Inflation is when the same units buy less.
- Banks sell trust: uptime, records, and sometimes reversal. That trust has rules — identity checks, delays, freezes.

Next lesson we name the exact design problems that made people want a public ledger. Still no shopping for coins.

lessons.title: The problems crypto was built to fix
lessons.content:
# The problems crypto was built to fix

Bitcoin did not appear because people were bored on the internet. It appeared after decades of trying to make **digital cash** — value that moves like a file, but cannot be photocopied — and it launched in 2009 after a global banking crisis.

This lesson names the **design problems**. It does not claim crypto solved all of them for everyone, everywhere. An academy that skips the problems will later sell you slogans.

## Problem 1 — a computer file can be copied

A photo can be copied. An MP3 can be copied. If digital cash worked like a photo, you could spend the same 50 units twice: once with a merchant, once with a second merchant.

That is the **double-spend problem**. In one sentence: **how do you stop someone copying electronic money and using it twice?**

Banks already have an answer. They are the referee. Only one database is allowed to be right. When you pay by card, your bank subtracts the amount. You cannot also spend those same units at a second shop unless the bank is wrong or offline.

Crypto’s bet was different: let thousands of computers share one public history, and make cheating more expensive than honesty. You do not need the engineering yet. You need the question: **if there is no bank to be the referee, who stops the photocopy?**

**Worked scenario.** You email a PDF invoice. The client can print it ten times. That is fine for a document. It is fatal for money. Digital value needs a single official history of “this unit already moved.”

## Problem 2 — you need permission to move value

To send money far away you usually need:

- an account that is open
- identity documents
- a corridor that is not blocked
- a weekday when the office is working
- fees that make a small payment look silly

When institutions work, this is a feature: fraud controls, consumer protection, a place to call. When they do not — capital controls, a frozen account, a weekend, a freelancer paid from another continent, a migrant sending a small remittance — the same design feels like a locked gate.

**Permissionless**, at the protocol level, means: if you can pay the network’s fee and broadcast a valid instruction, the software does not ask your surname.

Two honest warnings, immediately:

- Apps on top of crypto (an exchange, a random website, a “support agent”) often *do* ask your name. Do not confuse the **base network** with a company’s signup form.
- Permissionless is not a moral halo. It also means the network will not parent you if you send to a thief.

## Problem 3 — some payments reverse, some do not

Card networks often allow a **chargeback**: a customer disputes a payment and the scheme may reverse it. That protects buyers. It also means a merchant can lose both the goods and the money.

A completed international wire is closer to the opposite: recovery is a bank-and-legal story, not a button.

**Finality** means: after a payment has settled under the system’s rules, it is not a customer-care undo.

Bitcoin-style transfers are closer to **digital cash**: after the network has accepted them and later pages have buried them, there is no “dear support, reverse this.” That is power for settlement. It is danger if you send to the wrong place.

Academy rule from today, and we will repeat it until it is a reflex: **practice on tiny amounts.**

TABLE
System | Can someone reverse it? | Everyday use | How it fails
Card networks | Often a bank or scheme can | Shopping | Chargeback, freeze, “do not honour”
Bank transfer | Sometimes a bank or court | Local and some international payments | Delay, wrong account, compliance hold
Cash | Almost nobody | Face to face | Theft, bulk, distance
Public blockchain | Network rules, not a help desk | Open settlement | Lost secret, wrong address, scam
ENDTABLE

## Problem 4 — one company owns the history

If one office holds the only copy of the book:

- a hack can rewrite balances
- an insider can mint extra units
- an outage can freeze a country-sized pile of apps
- a legal order can freeze you, which may be legitimate law enforcement and may also be abuse — the design itself does not know the difference

A bank is a professional, regulated version of that single book. Public blockchains publish the history. Anyone can, in principle, check how many coins exist. That does **not** make the *price* honest. It makes the **rule-set inspectable**. Those are different skills. This course trains the second one first.

DIAGRAM
Private ledger                         Public ledger

  One institution’s database             Many independent copies
  You must ask “please update me”        Anyone can read the history
  If that office is down, you wait       One company is not the referee
ENDDIAGRAM

## Problem 5 — knowing your name is not the same as knowing the money is good

Traditional finance mixes three questions:

- **Who are you?** (KYC, passport, national ID)
- **Is this money good?** (clearing and settlement)
- **Are you allowed?** (compliance, sanctions, fraud checks)

A public blockchain mostly answers one question: **is this digital signature allowed to move these coins under the published rules?**

It does not know if you are a saint. It does not replace courts. Laws still apply to people and businesses. This academy will not teach you to hide from the law. Crypto is not a cloak of invisibility.

## What crypto does not automatically fix

Say these so they stick:

- It does not fix poverty by existing.
- It does not fix bad budgeting.
- It can make scams faster, because a completed send is hard to reverse.
- An unbacked token can still collapse in price.
- Clicking a random “airdrop” is not a job.

**Worked scenario.** A designer in one country is owed payment from a client in another. The bank corridor is closed until Monday, the fee eats a chunk of a small invoice, and a compliance hold asks for documents. That pain is real. Crypto networks were built to let value move with a fee to the network rather than a stack of offices. That does **not** mean the designer should skip identity law, tax law, or fraud caution. It means you can now see the design tradeoff: **open settlement versus institutional parenting.**

NOTE
If someone says “crypto fixes everything,” they are selling. If someone says “crypto is only crime,” they are not looking at the actual tradeoff: public rules, user-held secrets, hard-to-reverse settlement. Hold both thoughts.
ENDNOTE

## How this maps to Crystal Stones Academy

We teach the rails first so you can later look at a wallet screen, a BNB Smart Chain token, or a project website without drowning. Crystal Stones is one project on one network. It is not the definition of crypto. You will learn the map, then where that token sits, without being told to buy it.

## Say this out loud

- Digital money can be copied unless a referee — a bank, or a public network — agrees on one history. That is the double-spend problem.
- Moving value today often needs permission from offices. Base crypto networks do not ask your surname. Apps on top often still do.
- Hard-to-reverse settlement is both a feature and a way to get hurt.
- One private notebook is convenient and fragile. A public notebook is inspectable and unforgiving.
- Crypto does not parent you.

Next: Bitcoin’s origin, as history, not as worship.

lessons.title: Bitcoin’s origin, without hype
lessons.content:
# Bitcoin’s origin, without hype

On 31 October 2008, a person or group using the name **Satoshi Nakamoto** circulated a nine-page paper: *Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System*. The network started in January 2009.

You do not need to worship Satoshi. Nobody even knows who they were. You need to know what was new, what was borrowed, and what people still get wrong.

## Why 2008 is context, not a meme

Banks in several countries were failing or being rescued. Ordinary depositors watched institutions that held their salaries get special treatment they would never get. You do not need to become a historian. You need the feeling: **the bookkeepers were saved; many customers were not.**

The first page of Bitcoin’s chain even contained a newspaper headline about bank bailouts. Treat that as a timestamp and a political hint, not as a prophecy.

People wanted electronic cash that:

- did not bounce like an informal IOU
- did not require a card network’s permission
- had a public issuance schedule

## The one-sentence idea, then the slow version

One sentence: **Bitcoin is a network that lets people transfer a scarce digital token without a company in the middle, by agreeing on a shared history of transfers.**

That sentence contains three older tools glued together, not one miracle.

**1. Digital signatures**

A **digital signature** is mathematics that proves “the holder of this secret authorised this message,” without revealing the secret. It is older than Bitcoin. It is the difference between “anyone can type a payment” and “only the key-holder can authorise it.” Module 2 will go deeper. Today: it is proof of authorisation without a government name on the form.

**2. A peer-to-peer network**

**Peer-to-peer** means computers talk to each other without a required headquarters. Email and file-sharing used versions of this idea. Bitcoin uses it so there is no single “Bitcoin Inc” server that must approve a payment.

**3. A way to agree on order**

If two signed payments try to spend the same coins, the network must pick one history. Bitcoin combined **proof-of-work** (computers spending real electricity to propose the next page of the book) with a rule: honest computers build on the longest valid chain of pages.

The miracle people sell you is “magic internet money.” The actual invention is glue: old tools, stuck together, so there is a public notebook nobody privately owns.

## Why a cap of 21 million is a recipe, not a slogan

Bitcoin’s software is written so that only **21 million** coins will ever be created, released on a known timetable. About every four years the reward for producing a new page is cut in half. That event is called the **halving**. You do not need to trade around it. You need this: the issuance is a public recipe.

Whether 21 million is “good money” is a debate. Whether the cap is **auditable in software** is a fact. Fiat currencies do not come with a public recipe that says “this is the last unit that will ever exist.” That is not an insult to fiat. It is a difference in design.

TABLE
Claim you will hear | What is actually true
“Satoshi was a god” | Unknown author. The design is what matters.
“Bitcoin is anonymous” | Addresses are public. It is closer to a nickname than a mask. Investigators exist.
“Bitcoin is free to send” | You pay a fee to the computers that add the next page. Fees rise when the network is busy.
“One confirmation means done forever” | Wait for more pages on top. Exchanges often wait several.
“Bitcoin has a CEO” | No. Changes are social plus software. Messy, not corporate.
ENDTABLE

## How a Bitcoin transfer works, stripped of apps

Forget the logos. The skeleton is:

1. You hold a secret (we will call it a **private key** in the next module) that controls some coins recorded in the public book.
2. You write an instruction: “these coins, to this address, with this fee.”
3. You **sign** it. That signature is the proof it was you, without writing your government name.
4. The instruction sits in a waiting room. The waiting room is called the **mempool**. Ugly word. It only means “pile of valid-looking proposals not yet written into a page.”
5. A **miner** — a computer spending electricity to win the right to propose the next page — includes your instruction in a **block** (a page of the book).
6. Later pages are stacked on top. Changing your payment would mean rebuilding all those pages faster than the honest network. That gets expensive.

You will later do a cousin of this on BNB Smart Chain with a phone wallet. Same family of ideas, different engine.

DIAGRAM
Your secret key
        |
        v
Signed instruction (“pay this address”)
        |
        v
Waiting room (mempool)
        |
        v
A page is added (a block)
        |
        v
More pages on top (harder to undo)
ENDDIAGRAM

## What Bitcoin is not

- Not a company stock.
- Not a bank account with “forgot password.”
- Not a perfect tool for buying a bottle of water every time. Space on the pages is limited. Think of it more like a **settlement rail** than a coffee-app database.
- Not guaranteed profit. Price is a market. This course will not forecast it.

## Energy, said in class, not in comments

Bitcoin uses real electricity for proof-of-work. Critics say that is waste. Supporters say a global notebook that is hard to bully should cost something real, the way a vault costs steel.

You are allowed both thoughts: **security has a cost**, and **cost deserves scrutiny**. An academy that hides the argument is a fan club.

## Altcoins, in one paragraph so you are not lost

After Bitcoin, thousands of other coins and tokens appeared. Some copy the idea. Some add extra programs (**Ethereum** is the landmark for that). Some are jokes. Some are frauds. **Being “on a blockchain” is not a quality stamp.** The rest of Basic trains you to tell rails apart.

NOTE
Never send money to “Satoshi,” recovery agents, or people who say they can unlock a wallet for a fee. Bitcoin has no admin. Crystal Stones Academy staff will never ask you for the secret words that control a wallet.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Bitcoin launched after a crisis, as a public notebook with no company in the middle.
- The new part was the glue: signatures, a network, and a costly way to agree on order.
- 21 million is a software recipe, not a slogan.
- A send is: sign, wait, get written into a page, then buried under more pages.
- No CEO, no password reset, no guaranteed price.

Next: the most abused word in crypto — decentralised.

lessons.title: What “decentralized” actually means
lessons.content:
# What “decentralized” actually means

Decentralized is the most abused word in crypto. Projects stamp it on websites the way restaurants stamp “organic” on menus.

In this academy it has a testable meaning: **no single office can unilaterally rewrite the ledger, freeze every user, or change the rules without the network noticing.**

A system can be open in one layer and closed in another. If you do not separate the layers, a slogan will fool you.

## Five places power can sit

**1. Who keeps a copy of the book?**

If only one server in one company has the truth, that is a private ledger. If thousands of independent computers keep the same history, that is closer to a public one. Those computers are **nodes**. A node is simply a machine running the network’s software and (if it is a full node) checking the rules.

**2. Who is allowed to add the next page?**

If one operator always writes the next page, they are a central bank with extra steps. If many **miners** or **validators** compete or rotate, power is more spread. “More spread” is not “perfect.” Concentration can still exist — a few mining pools, a small validator set.

**3. Who can change the software people actually run?**

A CEO can ship an app update tonight. A public network changes only if enough people choose to run new software. Messy. Also harder to sneak a silent rewrite.

**4. Who holds most of the coins?**

If ten wallets own almost everything, those ten people *are* the economy, even if the software looks open. This is **holder concentration**. It is a different question from “how many nodes exist.”

**5. How do humans actually enter?**

If the only way to use the thing is one company’s app store, that company is still the gate, even if the chain underneath is public.

Bitcoin can be relatively open at the protocol and still be used mainly through an exchange. Crystal Stones can be a token on a public chain and still have a team, a website, and a marketing wallet. Both facts can be true at once.

TABLE
Layer | More centralised picture | More open picture
The book | One bank database | Many independent copies
Login | Email and password at a company | A secret you hold
Upgrades | CEO ships an update | Users choose which software to run
On-ramp | Only one broker | Many exchanges and peer trades
Token supply | An admin can mint forever | Fixed or public mint rules
ENDTABLE

## Why people want it

The hopes, stated as tests, not poetry:

- A manager cannot quietly delete you from the ledger because you argued.
- Supply is not only a press release. People can inspect the book.
- The network does not close at 5pm like a local branch.
- The base rules do not know your politics.

Those are hopes. Hopes are not guarantees.

## Why fake versions hurt people

- An **admin key** that can create new tokens out of nothing is a private money printer. “Admin key” means a privileged secret the deployer kept so they can mint, pause, or upgrade.
- A contract the team can silently **upgrade** is a company product. That can be legitimate — just do not call it unchangeable.
- If 90% of tokens sit in three wallets, “community governance” is a group chat.
- If the only place to trade is one website, that website *is* the product.

**Worked scenario.** A website says “fully decentralized token.” You ask five questions and get: the team can pause transfers, they can mint, liquidity sits in a pool they can empty, and the only market is their own site. The chain underneath may still be public. The *product* is not decentralised. You have just used the layer test. Keep it.

DIAGRAM
Someone says “we are decentralized”
                 |
     ----------------------------
     |            |             |
 Open public    Team can still   You still need
 chain          mint, pause,     a wallet, an
                or upgrade       app, an exchange
ENDDIAGRAM

## A practical test you will reuse all course

When a site says decentralised, ask, slowly:

- Can I verify the contract address from more than the project’s banner?
- Can the team pause transfers?
- Can they pull the trading pool (a **rug** — they yank the money and leave you holding a name)?
- Who can change fees or taxes?
- If the website dies, does the token still exist on the chain?

For Crystal Stones, the public BEP-20 contract on BNB Smart Chain, as the project publishes it, is:

**0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00**

Treat that as a **reference to verify**, not as a request to buy. Always check the address on a block explorer yourself. Scammers clone sites and change one character.

We have not yet taught you the explorer. That comes in Module 2. Today you only need the habit: **a slogan is not a test.**

## Spectrum, not a switch

Think of a slider:

- Left: cash in a box. You are the bank. Theft is on you.
- Middle: a fintech app. Convenient. Freezeable.
- Right-open: a public chain plus secrets you hold. Powerful. Unforgiving.

Professionals choose positions on that slider for different jobs. Sending rent is not the same job as settling a token between two programs.

NOTE
Holding the secret that controls coins is power and liability. A “decentralised” token sitting inside a centralised exchange account is, for practical purposes, an IOU from that exchange. Self-custody is a later course. Do not rush it with money you cannot lose.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Decentralised is a test of power, not a vibe.
- Ask who keeps the book, who writes the next page, who can mint, and who you must log into.
- Apps can be central while chains are open.
- Crystal Stones’ contract address is something to verify, not a buy order.
- Self-custody is later. Do not skip the queue.

Next: what crypto is not — immune-system training before any more vocabulary.

lessons.title: What crypto is not
lessons.content:
# What crypto is not

This is the most important lesson in Module 1. Everything else is vocabulary. This one is how you avoid becoming the story people tell after a loss.

The blockchain will happily settle a theft. The network is not your parent.

## It is not a job that pays you for existing

If a stranger offers any of these, it is theft wearing a suit:

- a “listing bonus” if you send USDT first
- a romance that needs you to help move coins
- a fake Crystal Stones, Binance, or NOWPayments support agent
- a chat admin who will “double your money in 45 minutes”
- someone who wants the **seed phrase** (the secret word list that controls a wallet) to “validate” you

There is no validation that requires those words. Anyone who has them can empty the wallet. We will unpack seed phrases slowly in Module 2. Today’s rule is simpler: **no human, including academy staff, should ever receive those words.**

TABLE
Pitch | Translation
“Guaranteed 20% a week” | They need new deposits to pay old ones, or they are lying.
“Send your seed phrase to validate” | They will empty the wallet.
“We are the official recovery team” | There is no recovery team.
“Pay gas in advance to this address” | Fake fee. Real networks take fees inside the transaction.
“The CEO privately told me the price” | Gossip is not a process.
ENDTABLE

## It is not automatically anonymous, legal, or tax-free

**Pseudonymous** means: the chain sees addresses, not necessarily passport names. That is not the same as **anonymous** (nobody can link you). Explorers show transfers. Exchanges in many countries share identity data with regulators. Local law still applies to fraud, securities, and tax.

This academy does not give legal advice. It tells you not to confuse “it happened on a chain” with “it happened outside the law.”

## It is not one coin

People say “crypto” the way they say “food.” Food includes rice, poison, and chewing gum. Crypto includes:

- Bitcoin
- Ether and other **native coins** (the home money of a network)
- **Tokens** on those networks (including Crystal Stones on BNB Smart Chain)
- **Stablecoins** like USDT — tokens designed to track a currency such as the dollar
- Experiments, games, scams

You will learn to name three things together, every time:

1. the **asset** (what are you sending — USDT? Bitcoin?)
2. the **network** (which road — BNB Smart Chain? Ethereum? Tron?)
3. the **address** (the destination, checked twice)

Mixing them is how people send USDT on the wrong road and never see it again. Same nickname on the bottle. Different planet.

**Worked scenario.** A checkout says “send USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20).” You hold USDT on Tron (TRC-20) because an exchange used the same ticker. You send. The letters still say USDT. The receiving contract on BSC never sees it. “Successful” on the sending side does not mean the receiver was paid. Same nickname. Wrong network. This is one of the most expensive beginner mistakes in the industry. The complete sentence is never “I sent USDT.” It is “I sent this asset, on this network, to this address.”

DIAGRAM
Wrong sentence: “I will send crypto.”

Right sentence:
  Asset:   USDT
  Network: BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)
  App:     a wallet you chose on purpose
  Address: 0x.... checked twice
ENDDIAGRAM

## It is not a substitute for reading

A whitepaper can be poetry. A Telegram with 50,000 members can be bots. A screenshot of “liquidity” can be borrowed for an hour.

Your process in this academy, every time:

1. Name the chain.
2. Name the contract (if it is a token).
3. Name who can change the contract.
4. Name how you would exit (who would buy it from you).
5. Only then talk about the story.

Crystal Stones’ public story is an **RWA** token. That acronym means **real-world asset**: a digital token whose story is tied to physical things. The project describes a BEP-20 asset on BNB Smart Chain, deflationary design, and backing claims around solid minerals, with additional talk of real estate and petroleum.

That is **their claim to verify**, not a certificate from this classroom that minerals sit in a vault under your name. Later courses teach how to read those claims. This lesson only plants the habit: **claim is not proof.**

## “Too late” and “too early” are both sales

“Too late, you missed it” is a sales tactic. “Too early, just buy now” is also a sales tactic. The adult position: **learn the rails before you size a bet.** Many people skip this and become the exit — the person who buys so that earlier people can cash out.

NOTE
Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for your seed phrase, private key, or a “verification deposit.” Payments for paid tracks, when live, go through the checkout we build — not a random wallet pasted in chat.
ENDNOTE

## Module 1 wrap

You now have:

- a model of money as ledgers
- the problems public ledgers attacked
- Bitcoin as a historical design, not a religion
- a working test for “decentralised”
- a scam filter

The quiz is not trivia for its own sake. If you cannot pass it, you will misread Module 2, where we open the engine.

## Say this out loud

- Three scam patterns: fake love, fake support, fake guaranteed yield. The chain will not save you.
- “Crypto” is a supermarket aisle, not one product.
- Always name asset, network, and address together.
- An RWA story is a claim. Claims need evidence.
- This academy refuses investment guarantees.

Take the quiz. Then we will walk, slowly, through what a blockchain actually is.

lessons.title: Transactions, blocks, and the chain
lessons.content:
# Transactions, blocks, and the chain

A **blockchain** is a shared ledger with strict rules for adding pages. The ledger is copied to many computers. Each **page** is a **block**. Each **line** on the page is usually a **transaction**.

IBM, banks, and every serious explainer use the same skeleton: record → agree → seal with a hash → link to the previous seal. We will walk that skeleton until it is boring. Boring is the goal. Magic is how scams talk.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate a proposed payment from a confirmed one, explain why pages are batched, and explain why linking fingerprints makes old history expensive to edit.

## A transaction is a proposed edit, not a finished payment

A **transaction** is a signed instruction the network has not necessarily accepted yet. Simplified:

“Address A sends 10 units to address B, and pays a fee to whoever includes this in a block.”

It is not complete when you tap Send in a wallet. It is complete when the network **accepts it into the official history**.

Until then it is a rumour in the **mempool** — a waiting room of valid-looking proposals. Ugly word. Picture an out-tray on a desk: signed forms waiting for the next official page.

If the network is busy, the form can wait. If the fee is too small on some networks, it can wait a long time. On BNB Smart Chain, waiting is usually short. Still, **Send is not settled.**

**Worked scenario.** You tap Send on a token transfer. Your wallet shows “pending.” A recipient who ships goods at that moment is taking the same risk as a merchant who hands over a laptop because a card terminal said “processing.” Settlement is a later state.

## A block is a batch with a seal

Networks do not write one line at a time to everyone on earth. They batch.

A block typically contains:

- a list of transactions
- a timestamp
- a reference to the **previous block’s hash**
- other header fields (nonce, height, Merkle root — names you can learn later; you do not need them to pass this module)

A **hash** is a fingerprint of the block’s contents. Change a comma, the fingerprint changes. Lesson 4 of this module will unpack hashes as tamper alarms. Today: the seal notices edits.

TABLE
Idea | Everyday picture | Chain picture
Transaction | A signed instruction, like a cheque | “Move these coins, signed by the key”
Mempool | Out-tray on a desk | Waiting to be picked
Block | A numbered page of cheques | Batch sealed with a hash
Chain | Pages glued in order | Each page names the previous fingerprint
ENDTABLE

## Why linking hashes makes history sticky

Block 100’s header includes the hash of block 99. Block 101 includes the hash of 100.

If you try to secretly edit a transaction in block 90, block 90’s hash changes. Then 91 no longer points at a real parent. You must rebuild 91, 92, … up to now, faster than the honest network. On a large proof-of-work or well-distributed proof-of-stake chain, that is the expensive part.

This is **immutability in practice**: not “cannot theoretically change,” but “economically stupid to rewrite deep history.”

DIAGRAM
Block 89  hash: a91f
        |
        v
Block 90  txs....  prev: a91f  hash: b22c
        |
        v
Block 91  txs....  prev: b22c  hash: c80e

Edit a tx in 90  =>  b22c becomes garbage  =>  91 breaks
ENDDIAGRAM

## Confirmations are extra pages on top

When your transfer is in the latest block, it has **1 confirmation**. Each new block on top adds one.

Exchanges wait for more confirmations on Bitcoin than on faster chains because a deeper burial is harder to undo. BNB Smart Chain is faster than Bitcoin. It is still not a joke to wait for an explorer to show success before you ship goods.

**Confirmation** does not mean “a human approved you.” It means “this many official pages now sit on top of the page that contains your payment.”

## Nodes and light clients

A **full node** stores and checks the rules — a complete copy of the book, or enough of it to verify.

Your phone wallet is often a **light client**: it does not keep the whole chain. It asks another computer for data. That helper is often called an **RPC** node (Remote Procedure Call — simply “a node you call for answers”). Convenient. It also means you are trusting that RPC a little. Advanced users run or choose RPCs carefully. You do not need to run a node this week.

## What people mix up, on purpose, so it stops

Three confusions wreck beginners the first week they open a wallet:

**Pending versus confirmed.** Pending means the proposal is in the mempool, or the wallet has broadcast it. Confirmed means a block producer included it. Deeply confirmed means more blocks sit on top. A merchant who ships at “pending” is taking credit-card-processing risk with fewer consumer protections.

**The wallet screen versus the chain.** Your app can lag, lie if it is malware, or cache an old state. The chain is the book. An explorer reads the book. When those two disagree, the book wins.

**“The blockchain” as one computer.** There is no single Bitcoin computer in one building. There are many nodes sharing one history. That is why a screenshot from one app is not the network, and why “the blockchain is down” usually means *your app, your RPC, or one chain among many* — not every ledger on earth.

**Worked scenario.** A freelancer sends a payment and immediately messages “check your wallet.” The recipient’s app still shows zero. Two honest explanations exist: the transaction is still in the mempool, or the recipient’s light wallet has not refreshed from its RPC. A third, dishonest explanation is a fake “sent” screenshot. The adult move is not an argument. It is: open the explorer, paste the transaction ID or the destination address, and read the official history. If the row is not there, it is not paid. Module 2’s later lessons will make that reflex mechanical.

This is the skill the rest of Basic is for: **you stop taking apps at their word, and you start taking public ledgers at theirs.**

NOTE
If this lesson still feels like a pile of new words, keep only four: line (transaction), page (block), glue (hash of the previous page), waiting room (mempool). Everything else in this module hangs on those four.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- A transaction is a proposal. It is settled when it is written into the official book.
- A block is a page of proposals with a seal.
- Pages name the previous seal so quiet edits break the glue.
- Confirmations are extra pages on top.
- Your phone wallet is often asking a helper computer, not storing the whole chain.

Next: the object that actually controls coins — keys.

lessons.title: Keys, addresses, and “your keys, your coins”
lessons.content:
# Keys, addresses, and “your keys, your coins”

If Module 1 was money, this lesson is **property law for the internet of value**.

On typical public chains, coins are not stored “in the app.” The chain stores balances (or UTXOs — unspent outputs, Bitcoin’s accounting style). Your **private key** is the power of attorney to move them.

People mix three objects. Mixing them is how funds disappear.

## The three pieces, defined

**Private key**

A huge secret number. Anyone who has it can sign “yes, move these coins.” This is the vault combination. If someone copies it, they can empty the account. There is no bank manager to call.

**Public key**

Mathematics derives this from the private key. You can show it. Other computers use it to check that a signature is real. Think of it as the lock on a door: people can see the lock. They cannot open it without the key.

**Address**

A shorter form you paste when someone should pay you. Like an account number, except there is no bank to call if you paste it wrong. On Ethereum-style chains (including BNB Smart Chain) addresses look like `0x` followed by 40 hexadecimal characters.

A **seed phrase** (12 or 24 ordinary words, also called a **recovery phrase** or **mnemonic**) is a human backup that can regenerate those keys. If you photograph it, you photographed your vault. If you type it into a “giveaway website,” you handed over the vault.

TABLE
Object | Share it? | If stolen
Private key / seed phrase | NEVER | Funds can be drained now
Address | Yes, when receiving | People can see you got paid; they cannot spend unless they have the key
Wallet app password | No | May lock the key on that one device — not a chain-level reset
Exchange email login | No | They can empty the exchange account; that is not the same as chain keys
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario — email versus a house.** Your email address is public enough to receive a message. Your email password must not be public. A wallet **address** is the email address of value. The **private key / seed** is the password — except there is no “reset password” link, because there is no company in the middle. A wallet **app PIN** is only the lock on that one phone’s drawer. Resetting the PIN does not reset the chain.

## Two ways to “have” crypto

**Self-custody**

You hold the keys. A carefully used software wallet. Later, a hardware device. The chain agrees you can spend because you can sign.

**Custodial**

An exchange or app holds the keys and shows you a balance. You have an account, like a bank. Useful for changing local currency into crypto. Also: exchange risk, freezes, phishing of the login.

Neither is morally superior. **Mixing them up is how people lose everything.** “I have Bitcoin on an exchange” means you have an **IOU** from that exchange until you withdraw to an address you control. An IOU is a promise in *their* ledger, not coins sitting in a key you hold.

DIAGRAM
Self-custody                            Custodial (exchange)

 Seed phrase → keys → address           Email / KYC → company ledger
        |                                      |
        v                                      v
 Chain agrees you can spend             Company agrees you can withdraw
ENDDIAGRAM

The slogan **“your keys, your coins”** means: whoever can sign with the private key can spend the assets. If you do not hold the keys, you hold a promise.

## How a seed phrase actually works (without the priesthood)

A seed phrase is not a password you invented. It is a human encoding of a large random number. Wallet software runs a standard (you will hear **BIP-39** — a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal that most ecosystems reused) to turn those words into keys.

Consequences that matter on day one:

- The words are the backup. The app is disposable. Uninstalling the app does not move coins. Losing the words without a copy does.
- Word order matters. The same 12 words in a different order are a different vault.
- A 13th “passphrase” some wallets offer is an extra secret on top of the 12. If you do not understand it, do not turn it on. People have locked themselves out with a forgotten extra word.
- Anyone who sees the words, even for two seconds on a camera, can copy the vault. There is no “they didn’t spend it yet, so it is still safe.” Assume spent.

**Worked scenario.** You buy a new phone. The old phone is dead. If the 12 words are on paper, you install a reputable wallet from the official store, type the words *into that wallet, once, offline as much as possible*, and the same addresses reappear. If the words were only in a photo album or a chat backup, assume they leaked. Create a new wallet, move whatever remains with a tiny test first, and retire the old one. That migration is a later course in slow motion. Today you only need the law: **the words are the vault.**

## Why an exchange login is not a key

An exchange email and password protect an account on a company’s servers. Two-factor codes protect that same account. None of that is a private key for coins on the chain — unless you withdraw.

While funds sit on the exchange:

- the company can freeze withdrawals
- a phishing site can steal the login
- the company’s own failure becomes your failure

That is not an argument against using exchanges. It is an argument against saying “I hold Bitcoin” when you hold a balance in an app. Precise language is a safety tool.

## Why mistakes are brutal

There is no “forgot private key” email. That is the point of removing the company, and it is the cost.

Common disasters, in the order we will keep repeating:

- Typing an address by hand and missing one character. Coins go to someone else’s door, or to a door nobody can open. **Copy, then check the first and last 6 characters.**
- Sending an asset on the wrong network (USDT on Ethereum to an address that was meant for BNB Smart Chain). Same nickname, different planet. Often unrecoverable.
- “Support” in chat asking for 12 words. The wallet empties in seconds.
- Malware that swaps the address you copied. You paste a thief’s address without seeing it.

NOTE
In a later Basic course (Wallets, Keys & Self-Custody) you will practise this slowly. Do not generate a seed phrase on a random website. Do not type a seed into cloud docs or chat. Do not use a seed to “unlock a bonus.” There is no bonus. Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for a seed.
ENDNOTE

## Smart-contract accounts (preview only)

On Ethereum-style chains (including BNB Smart Chain), some “wallets” are programs with extra rules. You still need a key to control them. Extra rules can help (**multisig**: 2-of-3 people must sign) or hurt (a hidden owner key). Park this. You do not need it to pass this module.

## Say this out loud

- The chain does not know your name. It knows keys and addresses.
- Address is how people pay you. Private key is how you spend. Seed phrase recreates the private key. App password is only the lock on that device.
- “I have coins on an exchange” means the company owes you, until you withdraw.
- Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for a seed.

Next: who is allowed to add the next page of the book — miners and validators.

lessons.title: Who keeps the ledger: miners and validators
lessons.content:
# Who keeps the ledger: miners and validators

Someone must propose the next block. If everyone writes at once, the notebook forks into arguments. **Consensus** is the rule for picking one valid next page.

You do not need to become an engineer. You need this sentence: **block producers are paid to follow the rules, and they compete or rotate so one office is not the central bank.**

## Two famous engines

**Proof of Work (Bitcoin)**

**Miners** spend energy guessing hashes. The winner publishes a block. Others check it is valid and build on it. Energy is the cost of attacking. To rewrite history you must out-spend the honest set of miners.

**Proof of Stake (Ethereum today)**

**Validators** lock capital as a bond. If they cheat, they can be punished (**slashing** — a protocol penalty that destroys some of the locked capital). If they are honest, they earn fees and rewards.

BNB Smart Chain is not Bitcoin mining. It uses a staked / authority-style design: a smaller set of validators, faster pages, cheaper fees.

TABLE
 | Proof of Work | Proof of Stake / validator nets
Who produces blocks | Miners with hardware | Validators with stake (and rules)
Attack cost | Energy + machines | Capital at risk + social control of validators
Energy use | High by design | Much lower
Familiar example | Bitcoin | Ethereum (after 2022)
ENDTABLE

## BNB Smart Chain, in honest beginner terms

Remember three names, slowly:

- **BNB Smart Chain** (people say **BSC**) is a **network** — a road.
- **BNB** is the **native coin** of that road. It pays the fee.
- **BEP-20** is the style of token on that road, the cousin of Ethereum’s **ERC-20**.

Crystal Stones’ token lives here as BEP-20. That does not make Crystal Stones into BNB. It makes it a token riding the BSC road.

BSC is more centralised than Bitcoin at the validator layer. That is a tradeoff: speed and low fees versus “as hard as Bitcoin to lean on politically.” Adults pick rails on purpose. We will not pretend every chain is equally neutral.

**EVM-compatible** means: it speaks the same contract language as Ethereum. Tools, wallets, and token standards look familiar. Compatibility is not identity. BSC is still a different book, with different validators and different fees.

## What “consensus” is actually deciding

Consensus is not a group chat vote about whether you are a good person. It is a rule for this question: **which page is the next official page?**

If two valid-looking pages appear at once, the network must pick. Different engines pick differently:

- Proof of work: the page that came with enough computational work, then the chain that honest miners extend.
- Proof of stake: the page that a scheduled (or elected) validator proposed, then the chain that honest validators attest to.

A **fork** is what happens when two histories exist for a while. Short forks happen. Deep, successful attacks are what large networks make expensive. You do not need to trade around forks. You need this: **your payment is not “the universe agreed.” It is “this network’s rule picked a history that includes your transaction.”**

That is why “it is on the blockchain” is an incomplete sentence. *Which* blockchain? *How many* confirmations? *Which* token contract?

## Why validator concentration is a real sentence, not an insult

When people say BSC is “more centralised than Bitcoin,” they are not calling it fake. They are saying: fewer independent block producers, more ability for that set to pause or reorganise under pressure, in exchange for speed and low fees.

Bitcoin’s cost is energy and slowness. Ethereum’s cost is gas that can spike. BSC’s cost is a smaller validator set. **There is no free rail.** This academy uses BSC because Crystal Stones lives there and because cheap, fast blocks are how beginners survive their first practice sends. We will not pretend that choice is ideologically pure. We will teach you to name it.

DIAGRAM
Users broadcast transactions
        |
        v
Block producer (miner / validator)
        |
        v
Other nodes check the block against the rules
        |
        v
If valid, they add it and gossip it on
ENDDIAGRAM

## Fees are bids for block space

You are not paying “Crystal Stones” when you move a token on BSC. You typically pay **BNB** as **gas**.

**Gas** is the network fee for computation and inclusion. The courier does not take the token as payment. The courier takes the road’s home money.

People lose funds because they hold a token but have zero BNB. The wallet refuses the send — or they follow a scammer who says “send gas to this address first.” Real gas is taken *inside* the transaction, not as a separate gift to a stranger.

Write this until it is a reflex:

**Token ≠ gas. Gas is the native coin of the chain.**

On Bitcoin, fees are in bitcoin. On Ethereum, fees are in ether. On BSC, fees are in BNB.

**Worked scenario.** A wallet holds 500 units of a BEP-20 token and 0 BNB. The owner tries to send the token. The wallet cannot pay the validator. Nothing moves. A stranger in chat offers “I will unlock your gas if you send 0.05 BNB to this address.” That is theft. The fix is to obtain a small amount of BNB through a venue you chose on purpose — never by paying a stranger’s “unlock” invoice.

## Finality is a spectrum

Some chains treat a block as done quickly. Bitcoin wants more burial. If a shop releases a phone at 0 confirmations, they are taking risk. Wait until an explorer shows success before you hand over something you cannot claw back.

NOTE
You do not need to become a miner or a validator. You need one habit: before you send, ask “what is the gas coin on this network, and do I have a little of it?” If the answer is no, stop. Do not send that gas coin to a stranger who offered to unlock you.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Someone must propose the next page or the book becomes an argument.
- Miners spend energy. Validators lock capital. Both are paid to follow rules.
- BSC is a faster, cheaper, more validator-concentrated road than Bitcoin.
- To move a token on BSC you still need BNB for gas.
- Fast and cheap is a tradeoff, not a free lunch.

Next: why forging a transaction is hard — without a maths degree.

lessons.title: Why a transaction is hard to fake
lessons.content:
# Why a transaction is hard to fake

Scammers fake *you*. They almost never fake the chain’s arithmetic. This lesson is why.

A thief cannot easily walk into a bank and write “pay me two million” on your page. They need your login, or a court, or a staff insider. On a public chain, they need your **private key**, or they need to trick you into signing.

## Digital signatures

Your wallet signs a message: “move X from my address.” Nodes check the signature against the address’s public key. Without the private key, you cannot produce a valid signature. That is not a password guess like “1234.” The space is enormous.

So the attack that works is **trick the human into signing** (phishing, malware, fake sites), not “hack SHA-256 with a laptop in a café.”

**Phishing** means: a fake site or message that looks official so you type a secret or click a signature you should not. The chain then executes honestly. Honesty of the chain is not protection if you authorised the theft.

## Hashes as tamper alarms

A **cryptographic hash** takes any input and produces a fixed-size fingerprint (Bitcoin uses **SHA-256** — a specific hash function. You do not need to compute it). Good hashes are:

- **one-way** — you cannot reverse the fingerprint back to the original
- **collision-resistant** — hard to find two inputs with the same fingerprint
- **chaotic** — one flipped bit wrecks the output

Blocks commit to their transactions with hashes (often in a **Merkle tree** — a way to fingerprint many transactions efficiently so you can prove one payment was in a block without sending the whole block). Change one payment, the fingerprint moves, peers reject the block.

TABLE
Attack | Why it usually fails on a healthy public chain
Invent a signature | Need the private key
Edit an old block secretly | Child blocks still point at the old hash
Print extra Bitcoin | Nodes reject blocks that break issuance rules
Replay someone else’s tx as new | Nonces / UTXOs make copies invalid
Lie in a screenshot | Screenshots are not consensus — check an explorer
ENDTABLE

## Explorers are your eyes

A **block explorer** is a website that reads the same public data nodes see.

- BNB Smart Chain: BscScan
- Bitcoin: sites such as mempool.space
- Ethereum: Etherscan

When checkout tells you to send USDT BEP-20, you should later see:

- the **from** address (yours)
- the **to** address (the one on screen, character for character)
- the **token contract** (USDT on BSC, not a random “USDT” scam token)
- a success status

Anyone can deploy a token named USDT or CRYSTAL STONES. The name is a sticker. The **contract address** is the identity. We will repeat this until it is a reflex.

A **token contract** is a program on the chain that stores balances and transfer rules. The human-readable name is decoration. The address of that program is the ID.

## Why “I already signed” is the moment that matters

On a website, you type a password and the company checks it. You can later call support. On a chain, you sign a payload and thousands of computers will execute it if it is valid.

That payload might be:

- a simple send
- an approval (permission for a contract to move tokens later)
- a swap
- a “permit” or typed-data signature some sites use so you do not even see a send

If you cannot explain what you just signed, you do not sign. That one rule prevents more losses than any antivirus slogan.

**Worked scenario.** A site says “verify wallet — sign this message, it is free.” Sometimes a signature is actually a harmless login. Sometimes it is a typed-data permit that lets a contract drain tokens. You cannot tell from the marketing sentence. You can tell from the wallet’s decode screen, from the URL you typed yourself, and from whether you needed to be there at all. Foundations does not ask you to verify anything with a signature. Later courses will show a real wallet UI slowly. Today: **unexpected signature requests are a stop sign.**

## Replay and why you cannot photocopy an old payment

On Bitcoin, coins are tracked as unspent outputs. Once an output is spent, a copy of the old transaction is not a new payment. On Ethereum-style chains, each address has a **nonce** — a counter of how many transactions it has sent. Replaying the same signed payload fails because that nonce is already used (on that chain). This is why “copy the transaction bytes” is not a money printer. It is also why sending on the *wrong* chain is a different universe: the nonce and the contracts do not carry over.

DIAGRAM
Phishing attack (common):
  Fake site  ->  you sign  ->  real chain executes honestly  ->  funds gone

Protocol attack (rare on large nets):
  You try to rewrite history  ->  honest majority ignores you
ENDDIAGRAM

## “Code is law” is incomplete

People say **code is law** to mean: the chain will execute a valid signature even if you were fooled. That is true of settlement. It is not true of society. Courts still exist for humans. Bridges still get hacked at the application layer. Smart contracts can have bugs.

So: **the base ledger is hard to fake; the apps around it are not automatically safe.** That is why we separate rails, tokens, and websites in this academy.

**Worked scenario.** A merchant is shown a screenshot: “payment sent.” A screenshot is a picture. Pictures are easy. The merchant opens the explorer, searches the destination address, and looks for a successful transfer of the *correct token contract*, in the *correct amount*, after the invoice was created. If that row is missing, they have not been paid. Explorers are the court clerk. Screenshots are not.

NOTE
Anyone can deploy a token named USDT or CRYSTAL STONES. The name is a sticker. The contract address on a specific network is the identity. If those two disagree, trust the mismatch — not the logo.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Signing with a key is not the same as typing a password into a random website.
- A hash is a tamper alarm: change a comma, the fingerprint moves.
- Explorers beat screenshots.
- A token’s identity is its contract address on a specific network, not its logo.
- Scammers fake people. They rarely fake the arithmetic of a large chain.

Next: one full send, start to finish.

lessons.title: What actually happens when you send crypto
lessons.content:
# What actually happens when you send crypto

We now stitch Module 2 into one sequence. Keep a real example: sending a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain. It could be USDT. It could be Crystal Stones. The movie is the same.

Sit with each step. This is the lesson people wish they had before their first painful mistake.

## Step 1 — unlock

You open a wallet app. You type a PIN or biometrics. That PIN is **not** the chain key. It is the lock on the drawer where the key lives. A well-built wallet keeps the private key from leaving the device. If the device is compromised, that protection can fail. Unlocking is local.

## Step 2 — name four things, not one

You must set:

1. **Asset** — what is being sent
2. **Network** — which road (here, BNB Smart Chain)
3. **Amount**
4. **Destination address** — pasted, then checked

If 1 or 2 is wrong, you are already in danger. “I sent USDT” is not a complete sentence. “I sent USDT on BNB Smart Chain to this exact address” is.

## Step 3 — the network fee

The wallet estimates **gas in BNB**. Even if you are sending a token, the courier is paid in the road’s home coin.

If you have the token but zero BNB, the film stops. Nothing moves. Scammers will now try a second film: “send BNB to this address to unlock gas.” That is theft. Real gas is charged inside the send, to the network, not to a stranger.

For tokens, you are not mailing a physical chip. You are telling the **token contract** — a program on the chain that stores balances — “reduce mine, increase theirs.”

## Step 4 — the irreversible human moment

You read the screen. You sign.

This is the moment. After this, “I didn’t mean to” is a feeling, not a button.

## Steps 5 to 8 — broadcast, wait, page, proof

5. An RPC helper hears the signed instruction and gossips it.
6. It sits in the mempool. Validators see it.
7. A block includes it.
8. The wallet shows success. The recipient must still verify on an explorer, not on your screenshot.

TABLE
If this goes wrong | You will see
No BNB for gas | Wallet error; nothing moves
Wrong network | Funds may be unrecoverable on the other rail
Wrong token contract | You sent a fake asset that only looks like the name
Wrong address | Likely gone
Too-low fee on busy nets | Stuck pending (more common on Ethereum than BSC)
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
You  --sign-->  Token contract on BSC  --update-->  Recipient balance
                 \
                  --> Gas paid in BNB to validators
ENDDIAGRAM

## Native coins versus tokens in this flow

- Sending **BNB** is a native transfer on BSC — moving the road’s own money.
- Sending **BEP-20 Crystal Stones** is a call to the token program. The project’s published contract is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Always re-check on the official site and explorer. Do not trust a chat PDF.

If you send Crystal Stones as if it were BNB, or send it on Ethereum, you are performing a different, often fatal, action.

The wallet UI may show both as “Send.” The chain does not treat them as the same action. If a recipient’s memo said “send BNB” and you send a token, they did not receive BNB. If they needed a specific token and you sent BNB, they received BNB — which may not be what they sell, and which may not be recoverable as the token.

**Worked scenario.** A checkout pins “USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)” and shows one address. You:

1. Confirm the wallet network is BNB Smart Chain, not Ethereum.
2. Confirm the token is the official USDT contract on that chain, not a copycat.
3. Send a tiny test first.
4. Open BscScan, paste the destination, confirm success, amount, and token.
5. Only then send the rest.

Skipping the test to save ten minutes is how people lose the whole amount.

## What this academy’s checkout will do later

A serious checkout:

- names the **only** network (we will say BNB Smart Chain BEP-20 for USDT payments)
- shows a fresh address or a hosted invoice
- confirms on-chain on the server
- then unlocks the course in our own database

Never skip the warning: **wrong network can mean loss.**

NOTE
Module 2 quiz comes next. If gas versus token still blurs, re-read the miners lesson. This mix-up is the number one beginner burn on BSC. Tiny test send before a large one. Always.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Unlock, name asset + network + amount + address, pay gas in BNB, sign, wait for a block, check an explorer.
- Token is not gas.
- Screenshots are not proof.
- The academy will pin one network on purpose when paid tracks open.
- Practice with tiny amounts.

You now have the engine. Module 3 is the map: coins, tokens, three networks, wallets, exchanges, and where Crystal Stones sits — still not a buy order.
