lessons.title: Coins vs tokens vs networks
lessons.content:
# Coins vs tokens vs networks

Beginners say “I bought a crypto.” Professionals ask three questions:

1. Which **network**?
2. Is this the **native coin** or a **token** on that network?
3. What is the **contract** (if it is a token)?

Those three questions are how you stop mixing planets that share a nickname.

## A network is a separate ledger with separate rules

A **network** (also called a **chain**) is a community of computers following one rule-set. Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Smart Chain are not three brands of the same bottle. They are different books, different fees, different histories.

Think of mobile networks: airtime on one carrier does not magically sit on another. Value on Bitcoin does not magically sit on BNB Smart Chain because a ticker looked similar.

## Native coins

A **native coin** is the home asset of a chain. It usually pays for security and fees.

- Bitcoin the network uses **BTC**
- Ethereum uses **ETH** (ether)
- BNB Smart Chain uses **BNB**

You cannot “deploy Bitcoin as a BEP-20” and have it still be Bitcoin. You can have **wrapped** versions, which are IOUs on another chain: someone locks the original and issues a representation. Wrapping is advanced. Do not start there. If you cannot explain custody of the lock, do not wrap.

## Tokens

A **token** is a contract on someone else’s chain. **ERC-20** on Ethereum. **BEP-20** on BSC. The contract stores balances and transfer rules.

Crystal Stones is a **token** (BEP-20), not its own layer-1 coin. That is not an insult. USDT on BSC is also a token. Tokens are how most project assets exist.

A **layer-1** is a base chain with its own consensus (Bitcoin, Ethereum, BSC). A token does not have its own miners. It rents the host chain’s security and pays that chain’s gas coin.

TABLE
 | Native coin | Token
Lives | The base chain | A contract on a chain
Examples | BTC, ETH, BNB | USDT (BEP-20), Crystal Stones (BEP-20)
Pays gas? | Yes, usually | No. You still need the native coin for gas
Created by | The protocol | A deployer publishing a contract
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
BNB Smart Chain
  native coin: BNB  (gas + validator economics)
  tokens:      USDT, Crystal Stones, thousands more
                 |
                 +-- each has a unique contract address
ENDDIAGRAM

## Why this saves you money

If a checkout says “USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)” and you send USDT on Tron (TRC-20) or Ethereum (ERC-20), you may never see it again. Same ticker. Different planets.

**Ticker** means the short nickname (USDT, ETH, BNB, CST). Tickers are not unique. Contracts on a given network are.

**Worked scenario.** An exchange withdrawal screen has a dropdown: network. You are tired. You pick the first USDT you see. The recipient gave a BNB Smart Chain address. You picked Tron. Two days later the recipient has nothing, the exchange says successful, and a stranger offers to “recover” it for a fee. There is usually no recovery. The asset was real. The road was wrong.

## Crystal Stones in this picture, still not a buy order

- Network: BNB Smart Chain
- Type: token, BEP-20
- Home coin for fees: BNB
- Identity: the published contract address, not the logo

If a wallet has Crystal Stones and zero BNB, the token cannot move. That is not a Crystal Stones failure. That is the road’s gas rule.

## Standards are formats, not quality stamps

**ERC-20** is a shared interface: a contract on Ethereum that implements functions like transfer and balanceOf in a way wallets expect. **BEP-20** is the same idea on BSC. **TRC-20** is Tron’s cousin.

A standard answers: “can a wallet display this and send it without a custom app?” It does **not** answer: “is this token honest, backed, or worth anything?” Anyone can deploy an ERC-20 named USD Tether lookalike. The standard made the sticker printable. The contract address is still the ID.

**Stablecoin**, restated: a token *designed* to track a currency such as the US dollar. Design is not a law of physics. Some are backed by reserves you can audit. Some are algorithmic experiments. Some are fakes using the name. In this academy, USDT on a named network is a *payment rail we may pin later* — not a lecture that every token called USDT is the same object.

**Worked scenario, slower.** You will hear “just send USDT.” Ask:

1. Which network? (BEP-20, ERC-20, TRC-20, something else)
2. Which contract on that network is the official one this recipient means?
3. Do I have the gas coin of *that* network?
4. Did I copy the address from the screen in front of me, then check first and last characters?

If you cannot answer those four, you are not ready to send. That is not cowardice. That is Foundations doing its job.

NOTE
Nicknames are not identities. USDT, CST, BNB, BTC are labels humans like. The network plus, for a token, the contract address, is the identity. If a checkout or a contact will not name the network, do not send.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Network is the road. Coin is the road’s home money. Token is a program on that road.
- Tickers are nicknames, not IDs.
- Crystal Stones needs BNB in the wallet to move.
- Wrong network is a common way to lose funds.

Next: three roads you will actually meet — Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain.

lessons.title: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Smart Chain
lessons.content:
# Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB Smart Chain

You do not need fifty chains. You need three landmarks.

We will give each road a job, a home coin, and an honest weakness. The point is not to pick a favourite. The point is to stop treating “crypto” as one rail.

## Bitcoin — settlement and scarce coin

- **Job:** move BTC and store a conservative, high-cost ledger.
- **Home coin:** BTC. Fees are paid in BTC.
- **Programs:** limited compared with Ethereum. Culture prefers simplicity: “don’t change it.”
- **Beginner use:** understand it as digital cash / settlement, not as an app store.
- **Weakness you should respect:** when blocks are full, fees can spike. It is not always the tool for a tiny payment.

## Ethereum — programmable contracts

- **Job:** run applications (tokens, on-chain exchanges, experiments) with a global computer model.
- **Home coin:** ETH (gas). Fees can be expensive when the road is busy.
- **Tokens:** ERC-20, ERC-721, and more.
- **Engine today:** proof of stake. Validators, not Bitcoin miners. You do not need the politics; you need “different engine.”
- **Beginner use:** many serious apps live here. Watch gas.

A **smart contract** is a program stored on the chain that runs when you send it a valid transaction. Ethereum made that model mainstream. Tokens are the simplest familiar example: a contract that keeps a balance sheet.

## BNB Smart Chain — EVM, speed, low fees

- **Job:** Ethereum-like apps with cheaper, faster blocks.
- **Home coin:** BNB.
- **Tokens:** BEP-20.
- **Why this academy names it often:** Crystal Stones lives here, and planned USDT checkout for paid tracks will pin this road on purpose so beginners do not guess.
- **Honest tradeoff:** more validator concentration than Bitcoin. You gain UX; you give up some “maximum neutrality.”

Pick the rail for the job:

- Hold and move BTC as a conservative settlement asset → Bitcoin.
- Use a complex Ethereum application → Ethereum, and hold ETH for gas.
- Interact with Crystal Stones or with this academy’s later USDT checkout → BNB Smart Chain, and hold BNB for gas.

Mixing those three jobs into one “send crypto” sentence is how people lose funds.

## How to choose a rail without becoming a tribal fan

You will meet people who say only Bitcoin is real, or only Ethereum is serious, or only BSC is usable. That is identity, not analysis.

A practical beginner rule:

- If the job is **hold a scarce native coin with the longest security story**, Bitcoin is the landmark.
- If the job is **use an application that lives as a contract**, you need an EVM-style chain. Ethereum is the original. BSC is the cheaper cousin this academy standardises on for practice and for Crystal Stones.
- If the job is **pay a specific invoice**, you use the rail the invoice named. You do not improvise a “cheaper” rail because a video said so.

**Gas**, restated per chain: BTC on Bitcoin, ETH on Ethereum, BNB on BSC. Holding a token on Ethereum without ETH is the same trap as holding a token on BSC without BNB.

**Explorer**, restated per chain: mempool.space (or equivalents) for Bitcoin, Etherscan for Ethereum, BscScan for BSC. Bookmark them. Do not Google “BscScan” and click the first ad. Phishing copies sit on ads.

TABLE
 | Bitcoin | Ethereum | BNB Smart Chain
Native asset | BTC | ETH | BNB
Token standard | Rare / different | ERC-20 | BEP-20
Typical beginner use | Hold / transfer BTC | Apps, tokens, DeFi | Cheap tokens, BNB ecosystem
Crystal Stones? | No | No | Yes — BEP-20 contract on BSC
Explorer (examples) | mempool.space | etherscan.io | bscscan.com
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
Choose the rail for the job

  Store BTC long-term     ->  Bitcoin
  Complex DeFi on ETH     ->  Ethereum (watch gas)
  BEP-20 token / low fee  ->  BNB Smart Chain
ENDDIAGRAM

## Bridges — a warning, not a tutorial

A **bridge** moves value between chains by locking on one side and minting a representation on the other. Bridges are a major hack target. Beginners should avoid them until they can explain custody and contract risk. This academy will not rush you across a bridge to look clever.

If a video says “just bridge it,” close the video. A bridge is a later, dangerous tool, not a beginner shortcut.

NOTE
Official Crystal Stones contract on BSC, as published: 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00. Verify on crystalstones.org and BscScan. We do not teach “send to any address in a pinned chat message.”
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Three roads, three home coins: BTC, ETH, BNB.
- Crystal Stones is not Bitcoin and not BNB. It is a BEP-20 token on BSC.
- This academy standardises on BSC for its token and planned USDT payments so you are not guessing roads.
- A bridge is not a next button.

Next: the shops on those roads — wallets, exchanges, and DeFi.

lessons.title: Wallets, exchanges, and DeFi on one map
lessons.content:
# Wallets, exchanges, and DeFi on one map

You now have rails. Here are the **venues** on those rails.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say who holds the keys at a wallet, at a centralised exchange, and at a decentralised exchange — and why a deposit screen has a network dropdown.

## Wallets

A **wallet** is software (or hardware) that holds keys or talks to keys. Examples you will hear: MetaMask, Trust Wallet, hardware devices (Ledger-style).

A wallet does not “contain coins” like a leather purse contains notes. The chain contains the balances. The wallet contains **credentials** to move them.

If you lose the phone but have the seed phrase on paper in a safe place, you can recreate the keys. If you lose the phone and the paper, the coins are still on the chain — and nobody can move them, including you.

A **hardware wallet** is a dedicated device that keeps keys offline and only signs when you confirm on its screen. It is a later skill. Do not buy one from a random reseller who “sets it up for you.” If someone else saw the seed, it is not your vault.

## Centralised exchanges (CEX)

A **centralised exchange** is a company: they custody assets, match buyers and sellers, and usually ask KYC. Easy on-ramps from local currency. You meet order books, deposit networks, withdrawal fees.

This is often how beginners first touch crypto. That is fine. The trap is the deposit screen: it asks **which network**. If you deposit BSC funds to a Bitcoin deposit address, you are back in the wrong-road story.

Crystal Stones’ site describes a Crystal Stones CEX as part of its ecosystem. Treat that as **project infrastructure to study later**, not as “withdraw blindly.” Confirm networks on the screen in front of you, not on social media.

## Decentralised exchanges (DEX) and DeFi

**DeFi** means decentralised finance: programs that lend, swap, or pool assets without a traditional teller.

A **DEX** is a swap shop made of programs. On BSC, PancakeSwap is the name you will hear. You keep your keys. The program holds **liquidity pools** — pots of tokens other people provided so swaps can happen.

Risks, stated plainly:

- fake tokens with similar names
- rewards that cannot last
- bugs in the program
- you signing a bad **approval** (permission for the program to spend your token, sometimes “unlimited”)

An **approval** is a signed permission: “this contract may move this token from my address, up to this amount.” Unlimited approvals are common and dangerous. If the site is evil, it can drain later.

TABLE
Venue | Who holds keys | Good for | Beginner trap
Self-custody wallet | You | Using chains, receiving | Seed theft, wrong network
CEX | They | Buying with fiat, liquidity | Wrong deposit network, phishing logins
DEX | You + contracts | Swapping tokens | Scam tokens, bad approvals
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
Local currency / USD
    ->  CEX  ->  withdraw BNB + token to wallet
                      |
                      v
              Wallet on BSC
                      |
          -----------------------------
          |                           |
     Hold / send                 DEX swap / apps
ENDDIAGRAM

**Worked scenario — a safe first month, not a trading plan.**

1. Create a wallet yourself. Write the 12 or 24 words on paper. Store the paper offline. Never photograph it.
2. Buy a little BNB on an exchange you chose on purpose (the Exchanges course will go step by step — do not improvise this tonight).
3. Withdraw a tiny test of BNB to your wallet address on BNB Smart Chain. Check BscScan.
4. Only then withdraw a token, still tiny, still the same network.
5. Do not visit a DEX in week one. Swapping is a later skill.

If you skip to step 5 because a group chat said “APY,” you are no longer studying. You are a customer of someone else’s urgency. **APY** means annual percentage yield — a rate. Unsustainable rates are a marketing device.

## Order books versus pools, in one page

A CEX usually uses an **order book**: buyers post bids, sellers post asks, the company matches them. You are trading against other customers, through the company’s ledger, until you withdraw.

A DEX usually uses a **liquidity pool**: someone deposited two tokens into a contract; a formula prices the swap. You are trading against the pool. If the pool is thin, the price you get can be terrible (**slippage** — the difference between the quoted price and what you actually receive). If the token is fake, the pool is a fake-token shop.

Neither venue is “the real crypto.” They are different machines. Foundations only asks you to know which machine you are in, and who can freeze you.

**On-ramp** means converting local currency or dollars into crypto. **Off-ramp** is the reverse. Most on-ramps are companies. They will ask who you are. That is not the chain “becoming KYC.” That is the door you used.

NOTE
Connect is a signature-shaped permission. A pretty website can still be a trap. Type the URL. Bookmark it. If a stranger sends a “wallet connect” link, that is the same family as “send your seed to validate.”
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Wallet = keys. Exchange balance = IOU until withdrawal.
- Deposit screens have a network dropdown for a reason.
- DeFi is not free money on a map.
- Do not connect a wallet to a link from chat.

Next: where Crystal Stones sits on this map — education, not a buy order.

lessons.content:
# Where Crystal Stones sits (education, not a buy order)

This academy exists because Crystal Stones funds education as a utility. That does not turn the classroom into a sales floor. We describe **what the project publishes**. We do not predict price. We do not tell you to buy.

If you came here only for a signal, this lesson will disappoint you on purpose.

## Placement on the map you already have

Walk it with the three questions from the coins-versus-tokens lesson:

- **Network:** BNB Smart Chain
- **Type:** BEP-20 token (not a layer-1 coin, not Bitcoin, not BNB)
- **Official contract, as published:** 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00
- **Category they claim:** Real World Asset (RWA) token

Open the official site. Copy the contract. Later, paste it into BscScan and ask: “does this page and that explorer agree?” If a chat message pasted a different address, trust the mismatch, not the chat. That is the academic use of this lesson.

## What RWA means, carefully

**RWA** means **real-world asset**: projects try to connect an on-chain token to off-chain things — invoices, property, commodities, minerals.

The easy part is creating a token. The hard part is **legal title, audits, who holds the physical thing, and who you sue if the story breaks.**

crystalstones.org describes backing primarily in solid minerals (they mention gold, lithium and more), with additional exposure to real estate and petroleum. It describes a deflationary design, a circulating supply figure in the 104 million range, a total supply of 135,000,000, buy/sell taxes, and an auto-burn on buys.

Those are **website / whitepaper parameters**. Your job in later modules is to ask how they are enforced on-chain: can taxes change? is minting closed? is liquidity actually locked?

This classroom does not certify mines. A classroom paragraph is not a receipt. A receipt would be legal title, custody, and audit you can follow.

TABLE
Question | Beginner answer after this lesson
Is Crystal Stones Bitcoin? | No
Is it BNB? | No. BNB is gas. Crystal Stones is a token on BSC.
Where does it live? | BSC, BEP-20 contract above
Does this academy prove the mines? | No. We teach you to demand evidence.
May staff DM a payment address? | No. Use in-app checkout only when paid tracks open.
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
Physical claims (minerals, etc.)     <-- legal / audit world
            |
            |  (must be evidenced, not believed)
            v
BEP-20 token on BSC  <-- you can verify transfers on BscScan
            |
            v
Utilities the project describes: CEX, Academy, on-chain transfers
ENDDIAGRAM

## Tokenomics is not a personality test

**Tokenomics** means the economic rules of the token: supply, taxes, burns, who gets fees.

- A **burn** destroys tokens, reducing supply if the rule actually executes.
- **Buy/sell tax** takes a percentage of a transfer for the project’s programmed destinations.
- **Locked liquidity** means the pool used for trading is restricted from being pulled for a stated period — if the lock is real.
- A **renounced** contract means the team gave up the admin keys. That can be safer against silent minting and also **unable to fix a bug**.

“Renounced” is not a halo. “Audit” is not a halo. Audits have **scope** — they check what they were paid to check. They are not insurance.

The project site mentions a smart-contract audit, locked liquidity, and a renounced contract. You should still open the explorer yourself in later practical lessons.

## What this classroom is for, relative to the token

Crystal Stones Academy is a **utility**: education funded as part of the project’s public story. The course sequence (Basic free, Intermediate paid as a bundle, Advanced later) is how we force real learning — quizzes gate modules, ranks track completion, Crystal Mentor answers study questions and must refuse investment instructions.

None of that is a reason to skip the three questions:

1. Network?
2. Native coin or token?
3. Contract?

You should be able to place Crystal Stones on the map you built in this course:

- It is not Bitcoin.
- It is not BNB.
- It is not “crypto” as a single object.
- It is a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain, with an RWA claim that lives in the legal/audit world, and with transfers you can watch on BscScan.

That sentence is the whole academic goal of this lesson. If you can say it without a buy or a sneer, you are done.

NOTE
The public site has also used large market-cap targets. We will not repeat targets as facts. Marketing is not consensus. Crystal Mentor, when you use it, must refuse investment instructions. So must this page.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 token on BNB Smart Chain with an RWA story.
- Website claim and explorer fact are different species.
- This classroom stays non-advisory on purpose.
- BNB is still the gas coin.

Last lesson of the course: how to keep learning without becoming prey.

lessons.title: How to keep learning safely
lessons.content:
# How to keep learning safely

You now have a beginner’s operating system. This lesson is how not to throw it away on the first chat group.

By the end of Basic, the aim is not that you can recite slogans. The aim is that you can open a project page, name the network, name the asset, refuse a seed-phrase request, and know what you do not yet know. Intermediate skill is the whole Basic track plus practice — wallets, exchanges, BSC, and safety — not this course alone.

## A 10-minute page-reading ritual

When you open any project site:

1. Write the **chain** in your notes.
2. Copy the **contract** from the official site, then search it on the explorer. Confirm the site and explorer match.
3. Check whether you need a **native gas coin**.
4. Find **who can mint or pause** (later course: read the contract tab).
5. Ignore price predictions in the first pass.
6. Look for how you **exit** (pairs, exchanges, lock status) without believing screenshots.
7. Only then read the story.

If a page will not give a contract, there is no on-chain asset. There is a story.

## What “intermediate” means in this academy

People use “intermediate” as a compliment. Here it is a checklist. After the full Basic track you should be able to:

- create and back up a wallet without photographing a seed
- explain self-custody versus an exchange IOU
- withdraw a tiny test on a named network and confirm it on an explorer
- refuse seed, gas-unlock, and guaranteed-yield pitches
- name Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 token on BSC with a contract you verify
- know that DeFi, bridges, and leverage are later, optional, and dangerous

This course — Crypto Foundations — is the vocabulary and the map. It is necessary and it is not sufficient. If you skip Wallets, Exchanges, BSC, and Safety, you are still a beginner with good notes.

TABLE
Green flags (still not advice) | Red flags
Contract + explorer match | Contract only in a PDF from a stranger
Clear network labels | “Send USDT” with no chain
Docs that admit risks | Guaranteed returns, countdown bombs
You can explain coin vs token | “Trust me I am in the team chat”
ENDTABLE

## What Basic unlocks next

Stay on rails:

- Wallets, Keys & Self-Custody
- Exchanges & Your First Buy (process, not a pump)
- Blockchain & BNB Smart Chain for Beginners (deeper BSC)
- Crypto Safety & Common Scams

Then Intermediate (paid track when priced): Ethereum, DeFi, tokenomics, markets, NFTs, DAOs — still with quizzes gating modules.

DIAGRAM
Crypto Foundations (you are here)
        |
        v
Wallets -> Exchanges -> BSC deeper -> Safety
        |
        v
Intermediate track (unlock as a whole when payment is live)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Rules that survive every cycle

- Tiny test transfers before large ones.
- No seed to any human.
- Bookmark official URLs; do not click sponsored ads for wallets.
- Crystal Mentor can help you think; it is not a financial adviser and must refuse investment instructions.
- If you are breathless, you are not studying. Close the app.

**Worked scenario.** You finish this course and a friend sends a link: “new Crystal Stones wallet connect, listing in two hours.” You do not connect. You open the official site you bookmarked. You compare the contract. You remember: urgency is a sales tool, staff will not DM a payment address, and this academy’s paid tracks — when live — go through in-app checkout. That is intermediate behaviour from a beginner who finished Foundations. That is the point.

NOTE
You passed from “crypto is a vibe” to “crypto is ledgers, keys, networks, and contracts.” That is the whole point of an academy versus a highlight reel.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- A ritual for opening a project page: chain, contract, gas, admin powers, exit, then story.
- This course sits at the start of Basic, not at the end of becoming intermediate.
- Speed is the enemy of self-custody.
- Asset + network + address. Token is not gas. Screenshots are not proof. Seeds go to no one.

quiz.question: Gas on BNB Smart Chain is paid in?

quiz.question: A native coin and a token differ because?
quiz.option_a: Tokens are always safer
quiz.option_b: A native coin is the chain’s home asset and usually pays gas; a token is a contract on that chain

quiz.option_a: The same asset on the same network

quiz.question: A centralised exchange balance is?
quiz.option_a: The same as holding your own keys
quiz.option_b: An IOU in the company’s ledger until you withdraw
